title: A stabilization time is a fitted number with an error bar, and the bars matter as much as the dots
summary: A burning pool approaches steady burning gradually. The time to reach 90 percent of the steady rate is a single-number summary of that rise. Eight runs give eight such numbers with intervals, and an ignition-aligned median curve shows the shape they summarise.

media.alt: Horizontal dot plot with eight run names on the vertical axis and evaporation stabilization time t90 in seconds on the horizontal axis from about 25 to 300 s. Each run has a dark dot with a grey error bar. A dashed vertical line marks the ensemble median of 208 s. Dots range from about 80 s for the lowest run to about 278 s for the highest, and bars range from narrow to over 170 s wide.

source.caption: Evaporation stabilization time, all 8 runs
source.note: Group explainer for the evaporation topic. Figure 24 summarises each run by one fitted time; figure 25 shows the pooled normalized burning-rate curve aligned to ignition. The fit model behind t90 is not stated on either figure.

read_the_figure.question: How long does the burning rate take to settle to its steady value, and does that time repeat from run to run?
read_the_figure.axes: Figure 24: x, t90 in seconds (evaporation stabilization time), about 25 to 300 s. y, the eight runs, listed in descending order of t90. Dot: the fitted value for the run. Grey bar: its uncertainty interval (the interval type is not stated). Dashed line: ensemble median, 208 s. Figure 25: x, time in seconds since ignition, 0 to 400 s; y, normalized burning rate r, with a dotted line at 1.0; dark line is the ensemble median, grey band the interquartile range across runs.
look_at: The dots: the lowest run is at about 81 s (MVI_8042), the highest at about 278 s (MVI_8033); the middle six lie between about 174 and 245 s.

The bars: MVI_8036 and MVI_8049 are tight (about 190 +/- 12 s and 220 +/- 12 s) while MVI_8040 and MVI_8042 span 60 to 175 s. Wide bars mean the fit is poorly constrained, not that the flame behaved erratically.
The dashed median at 208 s: which bars cross it. Five of eight intervals do (MVI_8036, MVI_8033 and MVI_8042 do not).
Figure 25: the rate is near zero for the first 90 s, rises steeply between about 100 and 250 s and then fluctuates around 1; the noise is larger once r is large.
The IQR band widens with time in figure 25: runs agree on the shape early and differ on the details later.
read_the_figure.proves: The eight runs agree on the order of magnitude of the stabilization time, a few minutes, and on the shape of the approach to steady burning. It does not show that the time is a reproducible property of the setup: two runs are far from the median with wide intervals.
if_wrong: A bar that spans the whole range of the other runs: the fit is not constrained by the data, for example because the record is short or the rise is noisy.
A very early t90 with a wide bar (MVI_8042): possibly the run started burning quickly, or the normalisation steady value was set from too little data; the figure cannot say which.
A normalized curve that overshoots 1.0 (figure 25 reaches about 1.1 to 1.2): normalisation uses an estimated steady value, and noise rides on top of it.
must_check: What the bars are: a fit standard error, a bootstrap interval, a confidence interval at what level.
How the steady value is defined and how long a steady tail was available.
What is being normalised: the 'burning-rate proxy' is a camera-derived quantity, not a measured mass loss, per the project description.
That every run is aligned to its own ignition instant before pooling.
That the median of the eight dots, not their mean, is what the dashed line marks.
as_drawn: Read by eye, about 5 percent: MVI_8033 about 278 s, MVI_8041 about 245, MVI_8032 about 226, MVI_8049 about 220, MVI_8037 about 196, MVI_8036 about 192, MVI_8040 about 174, MVI_8042 about 81 s.
The median of those eight values is (196 + 220) / 2 = 208 s, which matches the label on the figure.
Interval half-widths are about 17, 43, 67, 12, 24, 12, 87 and 54 s for the runs in the same order, from the bar ends.
In figure 25 the median curve first reaches about 0.95 near 238 s and mostly stays between 0.75 and 1.2 afterwards.

terms.meaning: The time after ignition at which the burning rate first reaches 90 percent of its steady value.
Shifting every run so that time zero is its own ignition instant, so that runs started at different clock times can be compared.
A burning-rate proxy divided by its steady value, so the plateau is 1 for every run.
The long-time plateau of the rate, estimated from the end of the record.
A range around the fitted value expressing how well the data constrain the fit. Its type (standard error, bootstrap, confidence level) must be stated.
The band from the 25th to the 75th percentile across runs at each time.
A dot-and-interval plot with one row per study or run, used to compare estimates and their intervals at a glance.

remember: t90 is a summary of a curve, not a measurement; the curve is what was measured.
If the approach is exponential, r = 1 - exp(-t/tau), then t90 = tau ln 10, about 2.3 tau.
An interval is part of the result: read the bars before the dots.
The median is robust to one extreme run; the mean is not.
A pooled median curve can look smoother or steeper than any one run.
Normalised quantities hide the absolute scale: ask what was divided by what.

understand.title: Why a time-to-90-percent
understand.text: The approach to a plateau never strictly ends, so 'when it is done' needs a threshold. 90 percent is a convention that sits clearly above noise and clearly before the plateau is fully reached.

understand.title: Why plot it as a forest
understand.text: One row per run puts the point estimates in order and puts every interval on the same axis. Averaging first would erase exactly what this figure shows: runs differ by more than their own uncertainty.

understand.title: What figure 25 adds
understand.text: The forest shows eight numbers; the aligned curve shows the shape they are numbers of. The two should tell the same story: the rise happens between roughly 100 and 250 s, and t90 values between about 170 and 280 s sit at its upper end, as expected for a time to reach 90 percent.

steps.title: Normalise by the steady value
steps.note: The proxy at each time divided by its plateau, so the plateau becomes 1 and runs of different intensity overlay. Here the proxy is not a mass-loss measurement.

steps.title: A simple model of the approach
steps.note: The simplest saturating curve, used only to define the idea of a time constant. The curve in figure 25 is more S-shaped, so this model is a teaching device, not the fit used for the figure.

steps.title: Time to 90 percent
steps.note: Solving for t gives 2.30 time constants; for example t90 = 208 s corresponds to tau of about 90 s under that model. Computed here, not read from the figure.

steps.title: Median and its tolerance to outliers
steps.note: The median of an even number of values is the mean of the two middle ordered values, here the 4th and 5th.

steps.title: Does an interval cross the median
steps.note: A run whose interval contains the ensemble median is compatible with it. This is a descriptive check, not a hypothesis test.

worked.title: Median and time constant from the dots
worked.problem: Using the eight values read from figure 24 (81, 174, 192, 196, 220, 226, 245, 278 s), compute the median and the time constant implied by it if the approach were exponential.

solution.text: Order is already ascending; with n = 8 take the 4th and 5th values.

worked.answer: Median 208 s, matching the figure's label, and an equivalent time constant of about 90 s under the simple exponential model.

analyze.q: MVI_8042 has t90 near 81 s but a bar from 27 to 135 s. Is it an outlier, or is it consistent with the others?
analyze.hint: Does its interval overlap the other runs' intervals?

analyze.q: Figure 25's noise grows after about 200 s while the IQR band also widens. What two different things could cause the larger scatter at high r?
The mean of the eight dots is about 202 s and the median 208 s. Why are they close and when would they differ?
analyze.hint: One low value pulls the mean down.

evaluate.q: Can the figure support the claim that stabilization time is reproducible?
evaluate.hint: What fraction of intervals is compatible with each other?

evaluate.q: What should be added to figure 24 before it goes in a paper?
evaluate.hint: Interval type, fit window, steady-value definition, and n per run.

create: Draw figure 24 again with the fitted curve of each run in a small panel beside its dot.
Design a protocol to find out whether the early run is a measurement problem or real: what would you repeat or vary?

checks.answer: The time at which the rate first reaches 90 percent of its steady value.

checks.q: If r = 1 - exp(-t/tau) and tau = 50 s, what is t90?
Two runs have the same t90 but one has a 10 times wider bar. How do they differ?
checks.hint: The bar describes the fit, not the flame.
checks.answer: The one with the wide bar is much less well constrained by its data, so its value is less reliable even though the point estimate is equal.

checks.q: Why is the median shown, not the mean?
checks.hint: One run is far from the others.
checks.answer: The median is little affected by the early run near 81 s; the mean is pulled toward it. With only eight runs one outlier matters.

checks.q: How would you make the pooled curve in figure 25 more informative?
checks.answer: Overlay the eight runs lightly under the median, mark each run's t90, and state how the rate was normalised.
